questions.prompt: Which argument shows that every quadratic p(x) = ax² + bx + c (real a, b, c, a ≠ 0) has exactly two complex zeros, counted with multiplicity?
questions.prompt_markup: Which argument shows that every quadratic p(x) = ax² + bx + c (real a, b, c, a ≠ 0) has exactly two complex zeros, counted with multiplicity?

choices.text: x² - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3) has two zeros, so every quadratic has two zeros.

By the quadratic formula the zeros are (-b ± √(b² - 4ac))/(2a). If b² - 4ac < 0 the square root does not exist, so there are no zeros; otherwise there are two, so a quadratic never has more than two zeros.
The graph of every quadratic is a parabola, and a parabola that opens up or down always crosses the x-axis in exactly two places, so every quadratic ax² + bx + c has exactly two zeros.
The quadratic formula (-b ± √(b² - 4ac))/(2a) gives every zero: two real zeros if b² - 4ac > 0, one zero of multiplicity 2 if b² - 4ac = 0, and two non-real conjugate zeros if b² - 4ac < 0.

questions.correct_answer: The quadratic formula (-b ± √(b² - 4ac))/(2a) gives every zero: two real zeros if b² - 4ac > 0, one zero of multiplicity 2 if b² - 4ac = 0, and two non-real conjugate zeros if b² - 4ac < 0.
questions.grading_note: Every case of the discriminant gives two zeros counted with multiplicity (for D < 0, √D = i√(-D) is a complex number). The others check one example, use a false graph fact (x² + 1 never crosses), or ignore complex zeros.

questions.prompt: A student says p(x) = x³ + x + 1 has no zeros because it does not factor with integers. Which statement is correct?
questions.prompt_markup: A student says p(x) = x³ + x + 1 has no zeros because it does not factor with integers. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The student is right: a polynomial that does not factor over the integers has no zeros.
It has exactly 3 real zeros, because the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says a polynomial of degree 3 has 3 zeros, and a polynomial with real coefficients has only real zeros.
It has 3 complex zeros counted with multiplicity, and at least one is real, because non-real zeros of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs.
It has 3 complex zeros counted with multiplicity, and all three could be non-real, because a polynomial that does not factor over the integers need not cross the x-axis.

questions.correct_answer: It has 3 complex zeros counted with multiplicity, and at least one is real, because non-real zeros of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs.
questions.grading_note: Degree 3 gives 3 zeros (Fundamental Theorem of Algebra); conjugate pairs make the number of non-real zeros even, so at least 1 is real. The others confuse "no integer factor" with "no zero", assume all zeros are real, or ignore conjugate pairs.

questions.prompt: Which argument proves that every polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients has at least one real zero?
questions.prompt_markup: Which argument proves that every polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients has at least one real zero?

choices.text: By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra it has n zeros counted with multiplicity, n odd. Non-real zeros come one at a time, so there is an odd number of them, and an odd number of non-real zeros leaves at least one zero that is real.

By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra it has n zeros counted with multiplicity, n odd. Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs, so there is an even number of them; odd minus even is odd, so at least one zero is real.

The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says that every polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 with real coefficients has at least one real zero; a polynomial of odd degree has degree at least 1, so it has at least one real zero as well.
x³ - 1 has the real zero 1, so every polynomial of odd degree has a real zero.

questions.correct_answer: By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra it has n zeros counted with multiplicity, n odd. Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs, so there is an even number of them; odd minus even is odd, so at least one zero is real.
questions.grading_note: Count zeros with the theorem and pair the non-real ones. The others check one example, misstate the theorem (it guarantees complex zeros, and x² + 1 has no real zero), or claim an odd number of non-real zeros.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra is correct?
questions.prompt_markup: Which statement about the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra is correct?

choices.text: It guarantees that a polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 has n complex zeros counted with multiplicity, but gives no method to find them.
It says that every zero of a polynomial with real coefficients is real, so a polynomial of degree n has n real zeros counted with multiplicity.
It gives a formula, like the quadratic formula, that finds the exact zeros of every polynomial of any degree.
It applies only to polynomials that factor over the integers, so it says nothing about other polynomials.

questions.correct_answer: It guarantees that a polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 has n complex zeros counted with multiplicity, but gives no method to find them.
questions.grading_note: The theorem is an existence and counting statement. The others claim a formula (none exists in general for degree 5 or more), claim real zeros (x² + 1), or add a false condition.
